title: Inflation rate jumps to 4.9% as Australia’s cost-of-living crisis intensifies
description:
Figure up from 4.3% annual rate in September and nearly double Reserve Bank’s official target of 2.5%

Surging fuel costs and the end of electricity rebates have helped drive inflation to 4.9% in the year to October, from 4.3%, as cost-of-living pressures peak in the lead-up to Christmas.

text: Surging fuel costs and the end of electricity rebates have helped drive inflation to 4.9% in the year to October, from 4.3%, as cost-of-living pressures peak in the lead-up to Christmas.
Alongside a 6.3% increase in fuel costs last month, the latest figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed electricity prices were 25% higher than a year earlier.

Rachael McCririck, the ABS head of price statistics, said the huge increase in power bills reflected the end of government subsidies, “which reduced household electricity costs last year but are no longer in place”.
McCririck said removing the impact of these “temporary shocks” provided a better idea of underlying price pressures in the economy.
But even here, the news was worse than expected. The Reserve Bank’s preferred trimmed mean measure of inflation – which takes out the most volatile prices – lifted to 3.8%.
Economists had expected it to stay at 3.6%.
The latest consumer price report come two days after Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, stood up in parliament to warn Australians that economic conditions would get worse before they got better.
Analysts are hopeful that inflation will ease through 2027 to be back below 3% in 12 months’ time, as the shocks of this year ebb away.
And amid fears of a more severe economic downturn, financial markets before the release of the latest worse-than-expected inflation data had been pricing in an RBA rate cut by August.
